lessons.title: Job Switches, Two Form 16s and What to Do When You Do Not Get One

children.text: Siddharth, a product analyst in Bengaluru, switched jobs on 1 October 2025. His first employer paid him ₹90,000 a month for six months. His new employer pays ₹1,40,000 a month. In June 2026 he receives two Form 16s, and both show zero TDS. He is delighted, until he enters both salaries in his return and the portal tells him he owes ₹78,780.
Nobody made a calculation error. Each employer did exactly what the law asks, based on what it knew. The problem is what neither of them knew.
Why a Job Switch Creates a Tax Gap

Each employer calculates TDS on the salary it pays you, as if that were your whole income for the year. So each one gives you the full standard deduction, starts the slabs from zero and applies the rebate. Here is how that played out for Siddharth under the new regime.

body.title: Show me the combined tax working

children.text: Taxable income of ₹13,05,000 under the new regime: ₹20,000 on ₹4 lakh to ₹8 lakh, ₹40,000 on ₹8 lakh to ₹12 lakh, and 15% of ₹1,05,000, which is ₹15,750. Slab tax is ₹75,750.
No rebate applies above ₹12 lakh. Marginal relief would cap tax at ₹1,05,000, the income above ₹12 lakh, but slab tax is already lower, so it does not help. Cess at 4% adds ₹3,030, giving ₹78,780.

body.text: Two employers can each deduct TDS correctly and still leave you with a large tax bill, because neither one sees your full year.

stats.label: Standard deduction
stats.context: Once per year, not per employer

children.text: The Fix During the Year: Tell Your New Employer
The law gives you a way to close this gap before it opens. When you join a new employer mid-year, you can declare your salary and TDS from the previous employer. For FY 2025-26 this was
Form 12B
, under section 192(2) of the 1961 Act. From tax year 2026-27 it is
Form 122
under section 392(4)(a) of the Income-tax Act, 2025, which merges the old Forms 12B and 12BAA.

Your new employer then works out tax on your combined salary for the year, subtracts the TDS already deducted, and spreads the balance over your remaining months. The previous salary shows up in your new employer's Form 16 Part B in row 1(e), reported total amount of salary received from other employer(s).

body.caption: Employer B's TDS with and without Form 12B

cells: TDS per month, Oct to Mar

events.title: Collect your final payslip
events.description: Note year-to-date gross salary, exemptions claimed and TDS deducted by the old employer.

events.title: Submit Form 12B (Form 122 from tax year 2026-27)

events.title: Check TDS went up
events.description: If TDS is still based only on the new salary, follow up with payroll.

events.title: Collect two Form 16s
events.description: One from each employer, each with its own Part A for its own period and TAN.

events.title: Match both against Form 26AS
events.description: Confirm TDS against each employer's TAN, then enter each salary once in your return.

body.text: Submitting Form 12B is not compulsory, and many people skip it because they do not want the new employer to see their old salary. That is your choice, but the tax does not disappear. If you skip it, pay advance tax during the year on the combined income. Otherwise you pay the balance when you file, plus interest for the shortfall in advance tax once your liability after TDS is ₹10,000 or more.

children.text: Filing With Two Form 16s
With both certificates in hand, the job is to combine them without double counting anything.
Part A from each employer:
Each has its own TAN and period of employment. The periods should not overlap, and any gap months should match when you were actually between jobs.
Salary:
Enter each employer's salary once. If the new employer's Part B shows your old salary in row 1(e), do not add it again on top.
Standard deduction:
Claim it once for the year, not once per employer.
Exemptions and deductions:
Under the old regime, if both employers allowed 80C, the combined claim is still capped at ₹1,50,000.
TDS:
Claim TDS against each TAN exactly as shown in Form 26AS.

body.title: Two Form 16s: before you file
steps: Confirm the period in each Part A matches your joining and leaving dates.
Confirm the TDS in each Part A matches Form 26AS against that employer's TAN.
Check whether the new employer's Part B row 1(e) already includes your old salary.
Add both salaries once, and apply one standard deduction.
Recalculate tax on the combined income under both regimes.
If tax exceeds total TDS, pay the balance as self-assessment tax before filing.

children.text: When You Do Not Get a Form 16 at All
There are three common reasons, and they call for different responses.

cells: No tax was deducted from your salary
Your employer is not required to issue Form 16, because it is a certificate of tax deducted.
Ask HR for a salary statement. Use payslips and AIS to report salary.
Tax was deducted but the employer has not issued Form 16
The employer is in default and can face a penalty of ₹100 a day under section 272A(2)(g) of the 1961 Act, capped at the TDS amount.
Write to HR in writing. Check Form 26AS for the credit and file using payslips.
The company has shut down or stopped responding
You may never get a certificate, and the TDS may not have been deposited.
Rely on payslips, bank statements and Form 26AS. Keep all evidence of deduction.

children.text: Form 16 makes filing easier, but it is not a condition for filing. You can report your salary from payslips and your bank statement, and claim whatever TDS appears in Form 26AS. AIS also shows salary reported by your employer in its quarterly TDS statements.

body.title: No Form 16: two very different situations

columns.label: TDS shows in Form 26AS
points: The employer deposited the tax and filed its statements
You get full credit when you file
Use payslips for salary breakup and exemptions
Form 16 is a convenience you can do without

columns.label: TDS missing from Form 26AS
points: The employer deducted but did not deposit or report it
Your return will show a credit mismatch
Section 401 (section 205) bars a demand for tax already deducted
Keep payslips and correspondence, and expect to contest any demand

body.text: Your last employer's full and final settlement, including items such as leave encashment and pending bonus, is part of your salary for the year. Check that it appears in that employer's Form 16, or add it from the settlement statement if you do not receive one.

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Pooja's balance due
body.prompt: Pooja earned ₹8,80,000 from her first employer (April to November 2025) and ₹6,40,000 from her second (December 2025 to March 2026). She did not submit Form 12B. Her two employers deducted ₹20,000 and ₹0 of TDS. Under the new regime with no other income, how much tax including cess does she still owe when filing?
body.explanation: Combined salary ₹15,20,000 minus one ₹75,000 standard deduction = ₹14,45,000. Slab tax: ₹20,000 + ₹40,000 + 15% of ₹2,45,000 (₹36,750) = ₹96,750. With 4% cess: ₹1,00,620. Less TDS of ₹20,000 = ₹80,620, before any interest.

body.title: How many standard deductions?
body.question: Siddharth's two Form 16s each show a ₹75,000 standard deduction under the new regime. How much standard deduction can he claim in his return?
body.explanation: The standard deduction is allowed once per year against total salary income, however many employers you had. Each employer shows it because each calculates TDS in isolation.

body.title: The job-switch form
body.textWithBlank: For FY 2025-26, an employee who joined mid-year could declare salary from the previous employer to the new employer using Form ___.
body.explanation: Form 12B was used up to FY 2025-26. From tax year 2026-27, Form 122 replaces it under the Income-tax Rules, 2026.

body.title: Farhan's vanished employer
body.scenario: Farhan worked at a Gurugram startup from April to December 2025. The company shut down in January 2026 and never issued Form 16. His payslips show TDS of ₹8,000 every month, ₹72,000 in total. Form 26AS shows only ₹48,000 against the startup's TAN, covering April to September.
body.prompt: What should Farhan do when filing his return?
body.modelAnswer: He does not need Form 16 to file. He should report his full salary from April to December using his payslips and bank credits, and claim the ₹48,000 of TDS that appears in Form 26AS. The missing ₹24,000 for October to December was deducted but apparently not deposited or reported. Under section 401 of the Income-tax Act, 2025 (section 205 of the 1961 Act), he cannot be made to pay tax that was already deducted from his salary, but the processing system will only give credit for what is in Form 26AS. He should keep his payslips, bank statements and any emails with the company as evidence. If a demand is raised for the gap, he can respond to it with that evidence. He should also add any salary from a later employer and check the combined tax, since the startup's TDS was calculated in isolation.

points: After a job switch, each employer calculates TDS as if its salary were your whole income, so TDS is often too low.
Declare your previous salary to the new employer: Form 12B up to FY 2025-26, Form 122 from tax year 2026-27.
In your return, enter each salary once and claim the standard deduction once for the year.
Match each Form 16 Part A to Form 26AS by TAN, and pay any shortfall before filing.
No TDS means no Form 16 is required. You can always file using payslips, AIS and Form 26AS.
If tax was deducted but not deposited, keep your evidence. You are protected from paying it twice, but you may need to contest a demand.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and uses FY 2025-26 new regime rates for individuals below 60 with no other income. Interest for shortfall in advance tax is not calculated here. For your specific situation, consult a chartered accountant.
